<reason>Both sides were competent and the clash was tight, but CON (A) built the cleaner path. A's core line — every recovery PRO cited (Maya Bay, the Icelandic canyon, poppy fields) came from closures, fences, permits, or road/shuttle measures, not from removing a pin — was never squarely answered; when pressed to name one site where de-promotion alone brought traffic below capacity, PRO called the question rigged and fell back on a general "promotion moves people" mechanism and on Amsterdam, which A had already distinguished (a city declining to spend its own ad budget is not a city asking platforms to strip data from others' posts). A's pressure question also extracted a real concession ("yes, it reaches the selfie"), which A then weaponized into "broader than advertised and weaker than advertised." PRO's best material — the complements-not-rivals reframe, gateless sites, and reversible-vs-irreversible weighing — was legitimate, and its closing cost comparison (blurred pin vs fences and tow trucks) was well framed, but A had already met the gateless-site point with concrete gateless tools and argued that cheapness is not a benefit if the tool stops no feet. PRO's charge that A attacked a nonexistent "instead of" motion was partly unfair, since A explicitly engaged the "what does the complement add?" question. Both sides had clipped turns, roughly offsetting. Clear but competitive win for A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.4–A4.6): answering B's "principled line" question by distinguishing a destination's own money and voice (Amsterdam) from a government request to edit other people's posts, then converting PRO's "reaches the selfie" admission into the case that the tool is simultaneously sweeping in reach and unenforceable in effect — leaving PRO's closing to rely on cost-cheapness rather than demonstrated efficacy.</best_rebuttal>
